title: How To Praise The First Week Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains how to apply SCM's core rule of giving only 'worthy' praise, defined as work or performance greater than a student has done before, during the first week of school when a teacher doesn't yet know a student's baseline. He resolves the apparent tension by pointing out that a new classroom's routines and procedures are themselves new learning for every student, which automatically qualifies as worthy of praise the first time it's performed correctly. He distinguishes common expectations, like entering the room properly, from academic skills like writing, noting that common expectations have a ceiling: once mastered, they're no longer praiseworthy because they've simply become the baseline standard. The article warns that continuing to praise mastered routines dilutes the meaning of praise and puts trivial compliance on the same level as genuinely exceptional academic work. It closes by suggesting a simple 'thank you' as the appropriate response once a routine is fully established.
points: Worthy praise is defined as work or performance greater than a student has done before, which naturally includes new classroom routines during the first week.
Common expectations, such as entering the classroom correctly, have a ceiling: once mastered, they stop qualifying for praise because they've become the baseline.
Continuing to praise already-mastered routines weakens the meaning and impact of praise for genuinely exceptional work.
Praising trivial compliance at the same level as outstanding academic work confuses students about what actually counts as achievement.
Once a routine is fully established, a simple 'thank you' is the appropriate response rather than continued praise.
quotes: Here at SCM we define it as work or performance greater than an individual student has done before.
In other words, it’s new learning. And new learning, no matter what it is, falls under the umbrella of “work or performance greater than a student has done before.
Common expectations are the procedures and routines required for an efficient, well-run classroom. The expectation—or standard—for doing such things is the ceiling on improvement.

One reason we don’t praise common expectations is that they (the expectations) aren’t worthy of it. It would be like being praised for using the automatic checkout at the grocery store. Once you know how to do it, you know how to do it.
It puts pushing in their chair or turning in their work correctly on the same level as writing the best essay of their life. It’s confusing to students and loses its meaning and impact.
